newsitem.title: USA: Farrakhan says treated like head of state abroad.
newsitem.headline: Farrakhan says treated like head of state abroad.

text.p: Controversial U.S. Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan said his recent tour of Libya, Cuba, Iraq, Iran, Nigeria and Sudan "was the greatest trip abroad ever by an African-American."
Appearing on CNN's "Late Edition" programme, Farrakhan defended his controversial world tour as aimed at benefiting American blacks. He said it was misportrayed by the media.
But in a separate programme, Vice President Al Gore sharply attacked Farrakhan and called his activities "un-American."

"Personally, I believe that what he has done and said is just completely outrageous," Gore told NBC's "Meet the Press" programme. 'He has promoted anti-Semitism, he has promoted division between people of different racial and ethnic groups. That's un-American."

Farrakhan said he planned to broadcast by satellite his "World Day of Atonement" rally at the United Nations Plaza in New York this week. It is taking place a year after the "Million Man March" on Washington that emphasised the responsibilities of black men.
Farrakhan said Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi and Cuban President Fidel Castro "perhaps will send us messages of solidarity" but stopped short of saying they would address the rally by satellite.

In an interview with Newsweek magazine, Farrakhan said he realised his trip last summer drew criticism, but said "there has never been a black leader that was so honoured and respected by heads of state and governments as Louis Farrakhan was."
"This is no joke," he said. "We came back with so many gifts from the governments and people that the captain of the charter plane had to tell us, 'You cannot bring any more gifts on the plane.'"
"Now why didn't the press say that -- that Louis Farrakhan was literally treated as a head of state."

While in Libya, Farrakhan accepted a $250,000 human rights award, an apparent violation of U.S. law which prohibits financial dealings with Libya. It has been on Washington's list of states that sponsor international terrorism since December 1979.
The U.S. Treasury Department has denied Farrakhan's application to receive either the $250,000 or $1 billion that Gaddafi had pledged to the Nation of Islam after meeting Farrakhan in January.

Farrakhan, accused by Jewish leaders of being an anti-Semite, told Newsweek he hoped to meet some Jewish leaders in New York. "We really need to sit and talk as civilised and intelligent human beings, and if they can show me where I am in error, then I accept that," he said.
Gore noted that an investigation into Farrakhan's travels abroad to openly hostile countries was underway.

He said it would be improper to politicize the matter by calling for revocation of Farrakhan's passport in the middle of the presidential campaign, but quickly added that there was "no hesitancy based on a fear of alienating Mr. Farrakhan."
